newsitem.title: USA: RJR Nabisco raises dividend, sets $200 million share buyback.
newsitem.headline: RJR Nabisco raises dividend, sets $200 million share buyback.

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. Friday raised its quarterly dividend and said it will buy back up to $200 million of its stock in 1997, double the amount authorised last year.

While the news was expected, it came a day after Carl Icahn sold his influential stake in the company and on the heels of a major pro-tobacco court decision this week, making RJR's external troubles seem more distant, analysts said.
The turn of events allows RJR to get back to the business of selling cigarettes and food, giving a boost to the company and tobacco industry in general, they said.
RJR's stock, which languished around $25 as recently as August, rose to a 12-month high of $38.875 this week. It edged down to close at $36.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Lawsuits were being filed seemingly everyday and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration was launching the regulatory initiatives against tobacco that began Friday.

At the same time, Icahn and Bennett LeBow, chairman of Brooke Group Ltd. had been accumulating RJR Nabisco stock with vigour in an attempt to unseat the board of directors and force a spinoff of the company's 80.5-percent owned Nabisco Holdings Corp.
On Thursday, however, Icahn said he had liquidated his 19.9 million shares of RJR Nabisco.

RJR said its board had voted to change the record date for the April 16 annual shareholders meeting to March 10 from March 3. That would allow new holders of the shares formerly held by Icahn to vote at the meeting, it said.

RJR said the board's authorisation of up to $200 million of stock repurchases was part of a 10-million-share buyback objective set by the board in 1996. It said the objective is tied to the realisation of RJR's operating plans over several years.
As the first step in that programme, in 1996 the board authorised the repurchase of up to $100 million of stock in the open market. The company bought back about 3.3 million shares during the year.

Analysts said the tobacco industry's chances of a victory in litigation by states and consumers improved after a federal judge in California tossed out San Francisco's Medicaid recovery suit against tobacco companies because of the similarities between that suit and the other 22 state Medicaid suits, they said.

"For management, it is sort of back to the basics now -- let's make money for our shareholders and let's return some of it to our shareholders," said Martin Feldman, a tobacco industry analyst at Smith Barney.
Feldman said the urgency of a Nabisco spin-off was diminishing as the parent company's stock price rises and shakes off the severe market discount that was almost entirely related to litigation woes.

With a price in the mid-$20's, the capital appreciation of RJR's stock after a spinoff would have been about a 75-percent gain, according to Feldman. "Today, the value of a spinoff is more like 32 to 33 percent," he said.

Paine Webber analyst Emanuel Goldman said the company is now "reasonably on track" to accomplish the turnaround in shareholder value that Chief Executive Steven Goldstone assured his shareholders was due when he took the job in the summer of 1995.
